idiom_name: kotlin.sequences sequence {} builder (or generateSequence) as the unfold + Sequence.fold as the fold
implementation_notes: kotlin.sequences is the library realization: the sequence { } builder with yield is the coalgebra (a restartable state machine), generateSequence(seed, nextFunction) covers the common no-yield shape, and Sequence.fold(initial, operation) or reduce is the algebra. Sequences are lazy, so the producer emits each element only when the fold asks for it and no List is allocated in between; turning an existing collection into a sequence with .asSequence() only adds laziness on top of data that is already materialized. Use the eager Iterable.fold (or a loop) when the input already exists and the intermediate collection is not the cost being avoided.
code_sketch:
fun countdown(n: Int): Sequence<Int> = sequence {   // coalgebra: lazy unfold
    for (s in n downTo 1) yield(s)              // suspension per element
}

fun factorial(n: Int): Long =                      // fold over the generator
    countdown(n).fold(1L) { acc, v -> acc * v }    // no List in between
pitfalls: Sequences are cold: the builder body re-runs for every terminal operation, so a generator with heavy setup or side effects repeats its work per fold - cache with toList() if the generated values must be shared.
A sequence derived from a List (.asSequence()) is element-wise lazy but the List already exists, so the allocation the pattern targets is not saved.
yield is only legal inside the sequence builder's suspend scope, and capturing the builder's continuation in an escaping lambda is a compile error - keep the unfold logic inside the builder body.
